task_description: The task is a multi-hop web-lookup over Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (LII). The team must (1) find the fifth federal-rules section alphabetically (Federal Rules of Evidence), (2) find the article within it that has 'witnesses' in the most rule titles as of 2021 (Article VI. Witnesses), (3) take the first rule of that article (Rule 601), and (4) report the single word that was deleted in that rule's last amendment. The gold answer is 'inference' — i.e., the deleted word was 'inference' (referring to the pre-restyling text of Rule 601 which contained 'inference' and was removed), not anything from the most-visible sentence change.
final_vs_expected: produced 'except' vs gold 'inference' — the team locked onto the most salient sentence rewording (except->unless) and never inspected the actual amendment/redline that deleted 'inference'.
primary_cause: Single-agent capability/research error: WebResearcher could not access the actual amendment redline for Rule 601 and guessed the deleted word from the surface sentence rewrite (except->unless), arriving at 'except' instead of the truly deleted 'inference'.
mast_rationale: 3.2 (no/incomplete verification): the Critic flagged that the exact deleted word was ambiguous and that the amendment removed a phrase rather than an isolated word, and explicitly requested evidence, but the team never obtained the actual 2011 amendment redline/Committee notes that would show the real deletion; verification of the core 'deleted word' claim was never completed. 3.3 (incorrect verification): the Critic in Turn 2 wrote 'If answering in one word, "except" is the best-supported deletion,' effectively endorsing the wrong answer as best-supported, and the Finalizer accepted 'except' with no reasoning at all. 2.6 (reasoning-action mismatch, mild): WebResearcher privately considered multiple candidate deletions ('except', 'as', changes to 'witness') and acknowledged uncertainty, yet published a confident 'the deleted word was "except"'.
trace_narrative: Turn 1 (WebResearcher, 5 rounds): correctly fetched law.cornell.edu/rules, identified Evidence as the fifth section alphabetically (Appellate, Bankruptcy, Civil, Criminal, Evidence), reasoned Article VI 'Witnesses' has the most witness-titled rules, and took Rule 601 as the first rule. It fetched the Rule 601 page but the rendered content was mostly site chrome/truncated; it never surfaced the actual pre-amendment text or a redline. In round 5 it privately brainstormed candidate deleted words ('except', 'as', 'witness'->'a witness') and admitted ambiguity, then published a confident answer: deleted word = 'except' (except as otherwise provided in -> unless these rules provide otherwise). Turn 2 (Critic, 1 round): gave a fair structural review — accepted the section/article/rule chain, correctly flagged that 'as of 2021' was unverified, that the 'most titles' claim lacked a count, and that the change was a phrase not a single word; but then concluded 'If answering in one word, "except" is the best-supported deletion,' endorsing the wrong candidate, and asked WebResearcher for evidence on the 2021 constraint and title count. Turn 3 (WebResearcher, 2 rounds): re-searched, confirmed Article VI listing and saw the live page now reads 'as amended to December 1, 2024' (not 2021), admitted it could not confirm the 2021 constraint or get a redline, and re-published the same 'except' answer. Turn 4 (Finalizer, 1 round): emitted 'FINAL ANSWER: except' with no reasoning summary at all.
open_ended_diagnosis: This is fundamentally a single-agent retrieval/capability failure, not strong inter-agent misalignment. The question hinges on the *deleted* word in Rule 601's last amendment. The gold answer 'inference' comes from the actual amendment redline/Committee-note diff of the rule text — a detail that lives in the amendment history, not in the current rule's headline sentence. WebResearcher never reached that content: its fetch_url calls returned navigation chrome and truncated bodies, and its web_search snippets only showed the current rule text plus the citation string '(Apr. 26, 2011, eff. Dec. 1, 2011.)'. Lacking the redline, the agent substituted the most visually obvious rewrite it could see — 'except as otherwise provided in these rules' becoming 'unless these rules provide otherwise' — and extracted 'except'. The whole team then anchored on this single unverified surface observation. The Critic performed real, useful scrutiny on peripheral claims (2021, title-count) but on the load-bearing claim (the deleted word) it accepted and even ranked the wrong answer as 'best-supported'. The Finalizer added nothing, rubber-stamping. So the dominant failure is capability (couldn't fetch the amendment diff) compounded by verification theater: lots of caveats were published, yet the central claim was never independently re-derived from a primary source.
reasoning_vs_published: WebResearcher's private reasoning was markedly more uncertain than its publication. Round 5 reasoning explicitly enumerated competing candidates: 'the most straightforward deleted word might be "except," which was replaced with "unless"' but also 'the deleted word could be "as"' and earlier 'competent to be a witness' altered from 'witness' to 'a witness'. Despite naming several possibilities, the published message asserted with confidence 'So the deleted word was "except"' — a lossy compression of genuine doubt into false certainty (mild 2.6 / unreflective-publishing). Crucially, none of the candidates the agent privately considered was 'inference', and the agent never reasoned about consulting the amendment's redline or Committee notes that contained it, so the gap here is a knowledge gap, not withheld knowledge — the agent did not privately know the right answer. The Critic's private reasoning ('note that the sources are supported or potentially unverified... provide accurate and reliable information') did surface into a substantively faithful published critique, so no distortion there; its failure was endorsing 'except' as best-supported (false-trust) rather than withholding it. The Finalizer emitted no reasoning summary and published only 'FINAL ANSWER: except', so there is zero private signal — it simply trusted the chain. The selector for Turn 4 even privately noted 'a critic pointed out an unresolved gap, which gives me pause' yet still routed to Finalizer, choosing to terminate over closing the gap (mild premature-finalization decision, but the answer would have been wrong regardless given the retrieval failure).
